title: Demand Letter Template Engine
description: Render a demand-letter template in a single left-to-right `while` scan — string state-machine shape, because we handle `{{...}}` tokens, dotted keys, and missing keys without a naive global replace.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Legal-tech engineers see template-render problems weekly — demand letters, settlement offers, intake forms — and the interview probe is always about robustness. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Spec-heavy problem — clarifying questions are the signal.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm writing `renderTemplate(template, data)` for legal documents. Tokens look like `{{client.name}}` — double braces, possibly dotted paths. I substitute each token with its value from `data`. Before I code, the questions that actually change the implementation:"

• Are dotted keys supported (`client.name`, `incident.date`)? Or only flat (`name`)?
• What's the contract on a MISSING key — throw, render empty, or a sentinel like `[MISSING:key]`? In legal docs the answer is almost always 'never throw, render a sentinel a paralegal can eyeball'.
• Whitespace inside the braces — should `{{ client.name }}` work the same as `{{client.name}}`?
• Can a value contain `{{...}}` itself? Are we re-rendering recursively or treating values as literal?
• Are there escape sequences (`\{{literal}}`)? Usually no for demand letters, but worth asking.
• Malformed templates — an `{{` with no closing `}}` — what should happen? Crash? Pass through literally?
sections.why: The missing-key contract is the load-bearing clarifying question. If the interviewer says 'throw on missing', the implementation collapses to a one-liner with `.replace` + a callback. If the answer is 'sentinel' — which is what legal-tech always wants — the implementation has to keep going past the gap, which is why this is a left-to-right scan rather than chained replaces. Asking 'can values contain `{{...}}`?' is the senior-tier question: it surfaces template injection. If you naively `.replace` and a user-provided value happens to be `{{password}}`, a second replace pass would substitute it — that's the kind of bug a senior engineer flags before writing code.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious version before discarding it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is `Object.keys(data).reduce((s, k) => s.replaceAll(\`{{${k}}}\`, data[k]), template)`. One line, looks clever. The problems show up fast:"

• Dotted keys don't work — `data` doesn't have a key literally named `'client.name'`; it has `data.client.name`.
• Missing keys aren't detected — if `data` has no `caseId`, the `{{caseId}}` token just stays in the output as-is. The reader sees raw template syntax in their demand letter. Embarrassing.
• Template injection — if `data.name = 'Bob {{amount}}'`, the next replace pass turns that into Bob's name AND the amount. You don't want a user-supplied value to control template behavior.
• Repeated tokens (same key twice) work, but order-dependence on `Object.keys` ordering is a latent bug.

"So I'll abandon the global-replace approach and do a single left-to-right scan: walk a cursor `i` through the template, find the next `{{`, copy literal text up to it, find the matching `}}`, resolve the key, append the value (or `[MISSING:key]`), advance past `}}`, repeat."
sections.why: Saying the brute-force out loud proves you're not just reaching for a fancier pattern because it sounds smarter. The template-injection point is the killer — most candidates never raise it, and an interviewer can immediately tell you've thought about adversarial input. Naming the four concrete problems with `.replace` also sets up the single-scan approach as the *inevitable* fix, not just a stylistic preference.

sections.title: 3. Spot the shape — string state-machine
sections.prompt: What's the structural property that picks the scan over replace?
sections.why: Naming the shape — string state-machine with a cursor that only moves forward — is what distinguishes this from 'I'm using a regex'. The cursor-only-advances property is the O(n) defense and also the no-template-injection guarantee: we never re-read what we already wrote. The null-guard inside the reduce is the dotted-key insight that catches careless implementations — a flat `data[key]` would just return undefined for `'client.name'` because no key with that literal string exists. Spelling out the THREE pieces (forward cursor, null-guarded path walk, sentinel-on-miss) is what the interviewer is grading.

sections.title: 4. Trace through a tiny example
sections.prompt: Walk a concrete template through the scan to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me run the L3 input through the scan. Template is `'Dear {{client.name}}, We demand {{amount}}. Ref: {{caseId}}.'` with `data = { client: { name: 'Jane Doe' }, amount: '$50,000' }` — note `caseId` is deliberately missing so we see the sentinel fire."

examples.input: tpl='Dear {{client.name}}, ...', data={client:{name:'Jane Doe'}, amount:'$50,000'} — caseId missing
examples.output: Dear Jane Doe, We demand $50,000. Ref: [MISSING:caseId].
examples.note: Shows the three behaviors: dotted-key resolution (client.name), straight-key resolution (amount), and missing-key sentinel (caseId).
examples.trace:
i=0  open=5 (`{{` after 'Dear ')  → out='Dear '
     close=18, key='client.name' → split=['client','name'] → reduce: data → data.client → 'Jane Doe'
     out='Dear Jane Doe', i=20
i=20 open=32 (`{{` after ', We demand ') → out='Dear Jane Doe, We demand '
     close=40, key='amount' → reduce: data.amount → '$50,000'
     out='Dear Jane Doe, We demand $50,000', i=42
i=42 open=49 (`{{` after '. Ref: ') → out='Dear Jane Doe, We demand $50,000. Ref: '
     close=58, key='caseId' → reduce: data.caseId → undefined
     out='Dear Jane Doe, We demand $50,000. Ref: [MISSING:caseId]', i=60
i=60 open=-1 (no more `{{`) → out += '.' (the trailing literal)
return 'Dear Jane Doe, We demand $50,000. Ref: [MISSING:caseId].'

examples.note: Smallest happy path — single flat token, no edges.
examples.trace:
i=0 open=3 → out='Hi ', close=11, key='name' → 'Eve' → out='Hi Eve', i=13
i=13 open=-1 → out += '!' → return 'Hi Eve!'

examples.note: Repeated token — each `{{a}}` is found and resolved independently as the cursor moves forward. No re-scan needed.
examples.trace:
i=0  open=0, close=4, key='a' → 1 → out='1', i=6
i=6  open=10, close=14, key='a' → 1 → out='1 and 1', i=16
i=16 open=-1, out += '' → return '1 and 1'

sections.why: The first trace is the one to narrate out loud — it shows all three behaviors (dotted, flat, missing) in one pass. The third example (repeated token) is the one that proves single-scan vs chained-replace gives the same answer on happy paths but stays linear-time and injection-safe. The cursor positions are the teaching: notice that `i` only moves forward, never backward, so we can't accidentally re-process inserted text. That's the structural guarantee the global-replace approach silently violates.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & failure modes
sections.prompt: Real-world inputs are messy — what would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging — most of these come from real legal-data uglies:"

• Missing intermediate object — `{{client.name}}` but `data.client` is undefined. The null-guard `(o, k) => o == null ? undefined : o[k]` catches this; without it, the second reduce step crashes on `undefined.name`.
• Whitespace in token — `{{ client.name }}`. The `.trim()` on the extracted key handles it. Paralegals who hand-edit templates will insert spaces; the renderer should tolerate them.
• Unclosed `{{` with no matching `}}` — malformed template. The `close === -1` branch copies the rest as literal and breaks the loop — no crash, no infinite scan, just visible garbage in the output that someone can fix.
• Token containing `{{` itself — like `{{outer{{inner}}}}`. The `indexOf('}}', open + 2)` finds the FIRST `}}`, which closes at `inner`. So the key becomes `outer{{inner`, which won't resolve, so we render `[MISSING:outer{{inner]`. Not pretty but predictable and not a crash. If you needed nested templates you'd use a real parser.
• Empty template `''` — `indexOf` returns -1 immediately, loop exits, returns ''. ✓
• Value of `0` or `false` or empty string `''` — these MUST render, not trigger the missing-key sentinel. The check is `val === undefined`, not `!val` — falsy-but-defined values like `0` go through `String(val)` and render correctly.
• PII inside template — the renderer doesn't inspect values, so SSNs / DOBs flow straight through. That's correct behavior at this layer; redaction is a separate pass. Worth flagging.
• Adversarial input — value contains `{{caseId}}`. Because the cursor only moves forward, this is rendered as a literal `{{caseId}}` in the output, NOT re-substituted. The single-scan structure is itself the injection-safety guarantee.
sections.why: The `val === undefined` vs `!val` distinction is the kind of bug that ships and embarrasses you six months later when someone's settlement amount of `0` renders as `[MISSING:amount]`. Calling out PII at this layer (and saying redaction is separate) is the legal-tech-aware signal — you're not pretending one function does everything. The injection-safety call-out tying back to the cursor-only-advances property is the senior move that closes the loop with section 2.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & memory
sections.prompt: Defend the bounds with the actual amortization.
sections.say:
"Time is O(n + k·d) where n = template length, k = number of tokens, d = max dotted-path depth. The cursor visits each char of the template exactly once via `indexOf` jumps. For each token, the dotted-path reduce walks d steps. In practice d is 1-3, so this is effectively O(n + k) — linear in template size.

Space is O(n + m) where n is the template and m is the rendered output. We could try to render in-place but strings are immutable in JS, so accumulating into `out` is the standard. Honestly for a demand letter this is trivial — templates are <10KB, output is <50KB. The interesting scaling question is per-document-times-millions for a bulk-send pipeline.

"For extensions: precompile if you're rendering the same template 1M times. Run the scan once, produce an array of `{type:'literal', text}` and `{type:'token', key}` segments, then per-data-instance just iterate the segments and resolve keys. Turns the per-render cost from O(n) to O(k), and you parse the template exactly once. Same template approach as Handlebars."
sections.why: The amortization argument is short for this problem — there's no nested loop to defend — so the wrap-up's job is to show you see the precompile optimization that production template engines use. Naming Handlebars (or Mustache) unprompted shows you know the production version exists and you've made a deliberate choice to write the simpler one for the interview. The bulk-pipeline framing also surfaces that you're thinking about how this lives in a real system, not as a one-off function.

sections.title: 7. Robustness & tests
sections.prompt: Legal docs care about correctness — how would you add tests?
sections.say:
"Tests I'd write before declaring this done — and the order matters, easy-to-hard:"

• Happy path — flat keys, dotted keys, mixed (the L3 example).
• Missing key — produces `[MISSING:key]` for every missing field, never throws.
• Falsy-but-defined values — `0`, `false`, `''` render as `'0'`, `'false'`, `''` (NOT as `[MISSING:...]`).
• Whitespace tolerance — `{{ name }}` matches `{{name}}`.
• Empty template, empty data — both return `''` cleanly.
• Repeated tokens — same key appears twice, both resolve.
• Malformed — `'{{unclosed'` and `'closed}}only'` both don't crash.
• Adversarial — `data.name = '{{ssn}}'`, output should literally contain `{{ssn}}` not re-substitute.
• Snapshot test — render a known demand letter against a fixture data object, compare to a checked-in golden output. Catches drift in any of the above without enumerating cases.

"In a real legal-tech codebase I'd also add a lint pass: scan the template for `{{key}}` tokens and warn if any key wouldn't resolve against the supplied data — surfaces missing-data bugs at author time rather than rendering [MISSING:...] at send time. That's the kind of belt-and-suspenders an audit-driven domain wants."
sections.why: Legal-tech interviewers always probe robustness because the cost of a bad demand letter is real — wrong amount, wrong client name, missing case ID. The lint-at-author-time idea is the senior touch: it acknowledges that a `[MISSING:key]` rendered in production is already too late, and shifts the check left. Snapshot testing as the catch-all is the framework-aware move — explicitly choosing it over enumerated cases shows you know which tool fits which problem.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the demand-letter renderer character by character. Watch the cursor `i` advance, the `out` buffer grow, and the missing-key sentinel fire for `caseId`. State panel shows `i`, `open`, `close`, the extracted `key`, and the running `out`.

yield { line: 2, label: `init out='' (will accumulate rendered text)`, state: { template, data, i, out } };
yield { line: 3, label: `init cursor i=0 (only ever advances)`, state: { template, data, i, out } };
if (++safety > 200) { yield { line: 4, label: 'safety stop', state: { template, data, i, out, returns: out } }; return; }
yield { line: 4, label: `loop iter — i=${i}, scanning forward for next \`{{\``, state: { template, data, i, out } };
yield { line: 5, label: `indexOf('{{', ${i}) → ${open}`, state: { template, data, i, out, open } };
yield { line: 6, label: `no more tokens — append tail ${JSON.stringify(tail)} and break`, state: { template, data, i, out, open } };
yield { line: 7, label: `copy literal chunk before \`{{\`: ${JSON.stringify(literal)}`, state: { template, data, i, out, open } };

yield { line: 9, label: `malformed — no matching \`}}\`, copy rest as literal and break`, state: { template, data, i, out, open, close } };
yield { line: 10, label: `extract key = ${JSON.stringify(key)} (trimmed)`, state: { template, data, i, out, open, close, key } };

yield { line: 11, label: `resolve via reduce — split=${JSON.stringify(key.split('.'))} → val=${JSON.stringify(val)}`, state: { template, data, i, out, open, close, key, val } };

notes: A left-to-right scan beats chained `.replace` calls: it handles repeated/overlapping tokens correctly in one pass and won't re-substitute text a previous replace just inserted (template injection).

Dotted keys like `client.name` resolve by `key.split('.').reduce(...)`, null-guarding each hop so a missing intermediate object yields `undefined` instead of a 'cannot read property of undefined' throw.
A missing key becomes `[MISSING:key]`, not a crash — a paralegal can eyeball a half-rendered letter and fix the gap; an exception just loses the whole document.
Time O(n + k·d), Space O(n + m) — n = template length; k = token count; d = max dotted-path depth (≤3 in practice, so effectively O(n + k)); m = output length.

questions.q: Why scan the template left-to-right instead of chaining `template.replace('{{amount}}', ...).replace('{{date}}', ...)`?
options: `String.replace` without `/g` only swaps the first occurrence, so repeated `{{key}}` tokens would be silently skipped
A single scan handles repeated/overlapping tokens in one pass and won't re-substitute text an earlier replace already inserted
Chained replace mutates the original `template` parameter, which would corrupt subsequent renders
`replace` would coerce the data values to RegExp objects, breaking on values containing `(` or `?`
questions.explain: Each `{{key}}` is found and resolved exactly once as the cursor moves forward. Chained replaces re-scan the whole string per key and can accidentally substitute into text a prior replace produced — a template-injection footgun if a value itself contains `{{...}}`.

questions.q: How does `key.split('.').reduce((o, k) => (o == null ? undefined : o[k]), data)` resolve `client.name`?
options: It joins the parts back with a dot and reads `data['client.name']`
It walks the path one key at a time — `data` → `data.client` → `data.client.name` — short-circuiting to undefined if any hop is null/undefined
It only works for two-level keys
questions.explain: `reduce` threads the object through each path segment. The `o == null ? undefined` guard means a missing intermediate (no `client`) produces `undefined` cleanly instead of throwing on `undefined.name`.

questions.q: Why does a missing key render as `[MISSING:caseId]` instead of throwing?
options: `String(undefined)` returns `'undefined'`, and rendering that into a demand letter is worse than the sentinel
A partially-rendered letter is more useful to a paralegal than a crash that loses the whole document
Throwing would leave the cursor mid-token, so the next call would resume in the wrong state
Legal-doc templates contractually disallow exceptions in render — a sentinel is the audit-trail-friendly alternative
questions.explain: Graceful degradation: the operator sees exactly which field is unpopulated and can fill it, rather than getting an unhandled exception that discards everything rendered so far.

questions.q: What does `template.slice(open + 2, close).trim()` extract for the token `{{ client.name }}`?
questions.explain: `open + 2` skips past `{{` and `close` stops before `}}`, giving ` client.name `; `.trim()` removes the surrounding whitespace so the key lookup tolerates `{{ key }}` spacing.

exercises.prompt: Resolve a dotted key against a data object via reduce, null-guarding each hop. Fill the blanks so it logs the nested value.

blanks.hint: fold the path segments into a single value
loose equality — catches both null and undefined
the initial accumulator — the root object

exercises.prompt: Find a `{{...}}` token by index and slice out the key. Fill the blanks so it logs the key name only.

L3.prompt: Render a demand-letter template: replace each `{{key}}` with its value from a data object (support dotted keys like `client.name`). A missing key becomes `[MISSING:key]`, never a crash.
L3.expectedOutput:
Dear Jane Doe,
We demand $50,000 for injuries on 2024-03-01. Ref: [MISSING:caseId].
hints: Scan with a cursor `i`: use `indexOf('{{', i)` to find the next token, append the literal text before it, then `indexOf('}}', open + 2)` for the close.
Resolve dotted keys with `key.split('.').reduce((o, k) => (o == null ? undefined : o[k]), data)`.
If the resolved value is `undefined`, append `[MISSING:${key}]`; otherwise `String(val)`. Advance `i` past `}}`.
